paper_design_summary: A theory paper. The authors build a Bayesian model in which users with heterogeneous preferences choose how much information to send to an AI, trading off output fidelity against communication cost, and derive propositions and theorems on homogenization (output variance below preference variance), a homogenization 'death spiral' when the AI is retrained on AI output, and the spread of AI bias. Numerical simulations of the model (Section 5, Appendix F) illustrate the results; there are no human participants and no empirical data.

studies.label: Bayesian model of human-AI interaction with numerical simulations (theory)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; no people are studied. The paper derives analytical results and simulates its model.
assignment.quote: To study this effect, we introduce a Bayesian framework in which heterogeneous users choose how much information to share with the AI, facing a trade-off between output fidelity and communication cost.

participants.who: No human participants. Users are a modeled continuum of types theta drawn from N(mu_p, sigma_p^2) (p. 8, Section 3).
participants.quote: Formally, there is a continuum of users of type θ ∈ Θ, denoting a user's specific preference about how to complete the task.

ai_tool.name_model: Stylized AI that forms a Bayesian posterior over user preferences; no real model is tested. Figure 1 shows two abstracts of the paper generated with ChatGPT GPT-4o as an illustration only.
ai_tool.how_used: Modeled: the user sends a normal signal of her preference; the AI returns the posterior mean (Eq. 2, p. 8). The user can instead do the task herself at fixed cost Gamma (Eq. 3, p. 9).

task.description: Abstract task with a one-dimensional preference over outputs; examples given are writing an abstract (p. 2-3, Figure 1) and a journalist writing a news article (p. 11, Example 1).

eligibility.reason: Theory paper with no human participants and no empirical data. Results are propositions and theorems about a Bayesian model plus numerical simulations of that model (Sections 4-6, Appendix F, PDF p. 49). The codebook lists theory papers in the screening report and omits them from the dataset. The authors state that user behavior with AI is 'difficult to study empirically' (p. 26, Section 7).

one_line_finding: In a Bayesian model of human-AI interaction, the variance of outputs is lower than the variance of user preferences when everyone uses AI and falls as the cost of human-AI interaction rises (Theorem 1, p. 13; Figure 3, p. 14), and retraining the AI on AI output can drive output variance toward zero, a 'death spiral' (Section 5, Figure 4, p. 16); no human data.
open_questions: Design class: the form has no 'theory' code. I used 'other' because 'model_only' appears to mean studies of AI output without people; a reviewer may prefer 'model_only'.
notes: All 50 PDF pages checked: main text pp. 1-29 (references pp. 26-29), Appendix A pp. 30-32, Online Supplement Appendices B-F on pages numbered e-1 to e-18 (PDF pp. 33-50). The only empirical-looking items are Figure 1 (p. 3, two ChatGPT GPT-4o abstracts used as an illustration) and the numerical simulations (Figures 4-9, pp. 16-22; Appendix F, base setting mu_p = 0, sigma_p = 1, M = 1001, T = 100). The literature review (p. 5) cites Doshi and Hauser (2024), Anderson et al. (2024), Padmakumar and He (2024), and Wang et al. (2023) as empirical homogenization studies; those papers may be worth checking as separate candidates. The file name says 2024; the document is arXiv 2309.10448 v4 of 6 Jul 2025; earlier versions are not on the document.
